flashcards.q: What two properties must the max-heap/min-heap pair satisfy for O(1) median access to be correct?
flashcards.a: Every element in the max-heap (small half) must be <= every element in the min-heap (large half), and the two heap sizes must never differ by more than 1.

flashcards.q: Why is two-heap insertion O(log n) while inserting into a kept-sorted array/list is O(n), even though both can find the insertion point via binary search in O(log n)?
flashcards.a: A sorted array requires physically shifting up to n elements to maintain sorted order after inserting at an arbitrary position, making the insert itself O(n) despite the O(log n) search. A heap only ever touches O(log n) elements (sift-up/down) per insert, with no shifting required.

flashcards.q: Why can't Sliding Window Median simply remove the expiring element directly from a heap in O(log n)?
flashcards.a: A binary heap only guarantees O(log n) access to its top (extreme) element; finding an arbitrary non-top element for removal requires an O(n) linear scan since a heap is only partially ordered, not fully sorted. The standard workaround is lazy deletion.

flashcards.q: What is lazy deletion, as used in Sliding Window Median?
flashcards.a: Instead of immediately removing an expiring element from a heap, mark it as pending removal (e.g. via a per-value counter in a hash map). Only actually discard it when it happens to surface at a heap's top during a later operation, checking the pending-removal count at that point.

flashcards.q: In IPO/Maximize Capital (LC502), why must project-unlocking be a loop rather than a single conditional check after each pick?
flashcards.a: A single profitable pick can raise available capital enough to unlock MULTIPLE previously-locked projects at once. The unlock step must repeatedly move newly-affordable projects from the locked min-heap into the affordable max-heap until no more qualify, not just check once.

flashcards.q: How does the two-heaps technique generalize from tracking the median to tracking an arbitrary percentile like p90?
flashcards.a: Instead of keeping the two heap sizes balanced 50:50, keep their size ratio at p:(1-p) for the target percentile p. The value at the boundary between the two heaps is then the running p-th percentile, still updated in O(log n) per insertion.

flashcards.q: Why do large-scale distributed monitoring systems typically use approximate sketches like t-digest or DDSketch instead of exact two-heap structures for percentile tracking?
flashcards.a: An exact two-heap structure built on one machine doesn't merge cleanly with an independent two-heap structure from another machine. Approximate, explicitly mergeable sketches trade exactness for bounded memory and the ability to combine results across a distributed fleet.

flashcards.q: Why is Median of Two Sorted Arrays (LC4) NOT a two-heaps problem, despite the word 'median' in its name?
flashcards.a: Both input arrays are already fully sorted and static -- there's no streaming insertion to justify building and maintaining an incremental heap structure. The efficient solution is binary search over the partition point in the shorter array, O(log(min(m,n))), strictly better than constructing O(m+n) heaps for a one-shot computation.

flashcards.q: How does Kth Largest Element in a Stream (LC703) differ from the Two Heaps pattern, even though both involve heaps and streaming data?
flashcards.a: Kth Largest uses a SINGLE min-heap capped at size k, retaining only the top k elements and discarding everything smaller -- it answers 'what are the k largest seen so far.' Two Heaps splits EVERY element into two balanced halves to expose the middle value -- a fundamentally different question requiring a balanced pair, not one bounded heap.

flashcards.q: In Python, why must values pushed into the 'small half' max-heap be negated, and what happens if you forget to negate them again when reading?
flashcards.a: Python's heapq module only implements a min-heap. Negating values on push simulates a max-heap (the most negative value, i.e. the largest original value, sits at heapq's top). Forgetting to negate again when reading the value back produces a silently wrong (negative) result rather than an error.
